lessons.title: The management functions in an abattoir
lessons.html:
Management is getting results through others

A foreman manages a whole shift or several sections. The classic management functions apply directly to an abattoir:

1. Planning

Planning sets goals and decides how to reach them. In an abattoir this includes the weekly slaughter plan agreed with procurement and sales, staffing per shift, maintenance windows, cleaning schedules and planning for seasonal peaks such as December and Easter. A good plan links daily numbers to chiller capacity, labour, and dispatch commitments.

2. Organising

Organising arranges people, equipment and materials. It covers the organisation chart, who reports to whom, job descriptions for each station, and making sure skills cover every critical point, including backups for absent workers.

3. Leading

Leading means directing and motivating people. A foreman leads supervisors and through them the line. It includes communicating the plan, resolving conflict, building a culture where hygiene and safety are non-negotiable and supporting supervisors when they apply the rules.

4. Controlling

Controlling compares actual results to the plan and corrects deviations. Typical controls are daily slaughter numbers, yield, condemnation rates, hygiene scores, temperature logs, overtime, absenteeism and incident reports.

Levels of management

LevelExampleFocus
TopAbattoir owner or general managerStrategy, investment, customers
MiddleProduction manager, foremanPlans, systems, coordination between sections
First-lineSection supervisorDaily work of the team

The foreman must translate top management goals into practical shift plans and give management accurate information from the floor.

lessons.title: Decision making and managing change
lessons.html:
Making good decisions

Foremen make many decisions every day, some routine and some unusual. A structured process reduces mistakes:

  1. Define the problem or opportunity.
  2. Gather facts: records, observations, input from supervisors and inspectors.
  3. Identify options.
  4. Evaluate each option against criteria: food safety, legal compliance, welfare, worker safety, cost and customer impact.
  5. Decide and communicate clearly.
  6. Implement and follow up.

Food safety, legal compliance and safety are not trade-offs. An option that breaks the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 or puts workers at risk is not an option, however cheap it is.

Example

A chiller compressor fails at midday with 200 beef carcasses still to be slaughtered. Options might include reducing the day's kill, moving carcasses to other chillers if capacity allows, delaying slaughter while an emergency repair is made, or arranging cold storage elsewhere. The foreman weighs chilling capacity and meat safety first, then cost and customer orders, and informs the inspector and management.

Managing change

New equipment, new procedures, new customers or new regulations all bring change. People resist change when they do not understand it or fear it. To manage change:

  • Explain why the change is needed.
  • Involve supervisors and key workers early.
  • Train before the change goes live.
  • Start with a trial if possible.
  • Monitor closely at first and fix teething problems.
  • Recognise those who help the change succeed.

lessons.title: Performance, risk and continuous improvement
lessons.html:
Measuring performance

What gets measured gets managed. Choose a small set of key performance indicators (KPIs) for your area and review them regularly with supervisors.

KPIWhat it tells you
Animals slaughtered per hourThroughput and line balance
Dressing percentage and trim lossesYield and dressing quality
Contamination findings per 100 carcassesHygiene performance
Hygiene audit resultsCompliance with the regulations
Lost-time injuriesSafety performance
Absenteeism and overtime hoursLabour management and cost
Customer complaintsQuality as the market sees it

Managing risk

A risk is something that could go wrong and harm people, product or the business. Identify risks, rate them by how likely and how serious they are, and plan controls. Typical abattoir risks include power failure, disease outbreaks that stop animal movement, loss of key skills, failed audits, injuries, and water supply problems. Controls might include a standby generator, multi-skilling, preventive maintenance and an emergency plan.

Continuous improvement

Use the plan, do, check, act cycle. Hold short daily meetings at the start of the shift to review yesterday's results and today's plan. Encourage supervisors and workers to suggest improvements. Small daily improvements in trimming, hygiene and line balance add up to large gains.

Key points

  • The four management functions are planning, organising, leading and controlling.
  • The foreman links top management goals with daily shift plans.
  • Food safety, legal compliance and safety are never traded off against cost.
  • Explain, involve and train to manage change.
  • Use a small set of KPIs and a risk register to manage performance.
